column4: Financial Industry ETFs Slump as Banks Report Mixed 4Q Earnings
column10: [Exchange-traded funds that focus on banks and asset managers are tumbling after a week of weak earnings and warnings of impending economic headwinds. Shares of three of the largest ETFs tracking the financial sector—the Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF), the Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH) and the Fidelity MSCI Financials Index ETF (FNCL)—all dipped 1.2% on Thursday after posting consecutive losses during the week.  Rough Ride for XLF, VFH, FNCLSource: Bloomberg Large asset managers reported a mix of fourth-quarter earnings results. JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America Corp. and Charles Schwab Corp. boasted year-over-year revenue increases as balance sheets were buoyed by net interest income. Other firms fared less well: Revenue at BlackRock Inc., the world’s biggest ETF issuer, plummeted 18% year over year, and Goldman Sachs Inc. posted its largest earnings miss in a decade. All five companies are within the top 10 holdings in XLF, VFH and FNCL. Still, executives are cautioning of a coming economic downturn, despite stocks bouncing back after 2022’s double-digit declines. “We still do not know the ultimate effect of the headwinds coming from geopolitical tensions,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said during the bank’s fourth-quarter earnings call last week. He listed impediments to growth such as “war in Ukraine, the vulnerable state of energy and food supplies, persistent inflation that is eroding purchasing power and has pushed interest rates higher, and the unprecedented quantitative tightening.” In preparation, banks are bolstering loan loss provisions, cash reserves that banks set aside to cover problem loans that are unlikely to see repayment. Bank of America, the second largest bank in the U.S., has set aside $403 million to cover possible bad loans, with CEO Brian Moynihan alluding to an "increasingly slowing economic environment” during the firm’s quarterly earnings call with analysts and investors. column4: Financial Industry ETFs Slump as Banks Report Mixed 4Q Earnings
column10: [Exchange-traded funds that focus on banks and asset managers are tumbling after a week of weak earnings and warnings of impending economic headwinds. Shares of three of the largest ETFs tracking the financial sector—the Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF), the Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH) and the Fidelity MSCI Financials Index ETF (FNCL)—all dipped 1.2% on Thursday after posting consecutive losses during the week.  Rough Ride for XLF, VFH, FNCLSource: Bloomberg Large asset managers reported a mix of fourth-quarter earnings results. JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America Corp. and Charles Schwab Corp. boasted year-over-year revenue increases as balance sheets were buoyed by net interest income. Other firms fared less well: Revenue at BlackRock Inc., the world’s biggest ETF issuer, plummeted 18% year over year, and Goldman Sachs Inc. posted its largest earnings miss in a decade. All five companies are within the top 10 holdings in XLF, VFH and FNCL. Still, executives are cautioning of a coming economic downturn, despite stocks bouncing back after 2022’s double-digit declines. “We still do not know the ultimate effect of the headwinds coming from geopolitical tensions,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said during the bank’s fourth-quarter earnings call last week. He listed impediments to growth such as “war in Ukraine, the vulnerable state of energy and food supplies, persistent inflation that is eroding purchasing power and has pushed interest rates higher, and the unprecedented quantitative tightening.” In preparation, banks are bolstering loan loss provisions, cash reserves that banks set aside to cover problem loans that are unlikely to see repayment. Bank of America, the second largest bank in the U.S., has set aside $403 million to cover possible bad loans, with CEO Brian Moynihan alluding to an "increasingly slowing economic environment” during the firm’s quarterly earnings call with analysts and investors. column4: The 2023 investment narrative is already diverging from 2022: Morning Brief
column10: [This article first appeared in the Morning Brief. Get the Morning Brief sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Friday by 6:30 a.m. ET. SubscribeThursday, January 19, 2023Today's newsletter is by Jared Blikre, a reporter focused on the markets on Yahoo Finance. Follow him on Twitter @SPYJared. Read this and more market news on the go with the Yahoo Finance App.Despite Wednesday's losses in the major U.S. indexes, stocks are flying out of the gate in 2023.The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) and S&P 500 (^GSPC) are having their best start to a year since 2019.And in enjoying these gains in the new year, stocks are diverging from the trends that emerged in the second half of 2022. A move that has important implications for investors.Start with the biggest loser of the day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI), which was down 1.81%, or 614 points, on Wednesday, its worst showing in over a month. As of late December, the Dow had outperformed the Nasdaq by 20 percentage points — the most since the dot-com bubble crash two decades prior.Despite this outperformance, however, the Dow ended 2022 down nearly 9%. There were few places for investors to hide in 2022.But Wednesday, the Nasdaq outperformed the Dow by 57 basis points. Particularly notable coming on such a negative day for the market. In the first 11 trading days of the year, the Nasdaq is already up 4.69% compared to the Dow's meager 0.45% gain.If we dive inside the benchmark S&P 500 and look at relative sector performance, 2023's year-to-date sector chart is nearly the inverse of 2022.S&P 500 Sector performance year-to-date through Jan. 18., 2023.(Source: Yahoo Finance)Last year's second-worst-performing sector is this year's best: Consumer Discretionary (XLY).Helping matters are the sector's two largest megacap components — Amazon (AMZN) and Tesla (TSLA) — which are both nicely positive so far in 2023, gaining a little over 4% each.The two other sectors besides consumer discretionary that house some of the market's biggest names — Tech (XLK) and Communication Services (XLC) — are also serving as leaders this year.Story continuesAnd let's not gloss over the strength in Real Estate (XLRE), which is up more than 5% after having just endured one of the most challenging housing markets in a generation last year. Another big narrative shift after 2022.On the flip side, those red sectors in the above heat map — Utilities (XLU), Health Care (XLV), and Consumer Staples (XLP) — were the least-bad sectors after Energy last year. These sectors are also commonly referred to as defensive areas of the market for investors to find shelter in a storm. In the 2023 market, however, it seems safe trades aren't quite safe.The bond market is also confirming moves back into these formerly unloved, growthy areas of the market that took the biggest hits a year ago.On Wednesday, the yield 10-year on U.S. Treasury notes (^TNX) plummeted 16 basis points to 3.375%, a four-month low. All else equal, sinking bond yields favor growth stocks that depend on lower interest rates.And although buying bonds is often seen as investors fleeing to safety, right now the bond bid appears firmly part of a risk on trade.Finally, throw in Wednesday's market reaction to economic news.December retail sales surprised to the downside with a drop of 1.1%, which follows a similar negative print in November. Investors seem to be pricing in this objectively bad news for what it is — bad news — instead of trying to play 4D chess with Jay Powell and the Federal Reserve.Speaking of the Fed, the market's new favorite macro risk assets, bitcoin (BTC-USD) and ethereum (ETH-USD), are each up about 25% this year. Bitcoin and crypto have been particularly volatile around important Fed decisions and inflation data — leading risk markets to the upside at times, and downside at others.Bottom line: Bitcoin is a clear leader this year among the "fringier" parts of the markets, and, currently, the direction is up.Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Returns YTDNow, some of these pockets of the markets have been exhibiting strength since late last year. Under different leadership, this could change.But this is a market starting to show the hands of winners over losers.As Steven Strazza, director of research at All Star Charts tweeted this week: "Breakouts are sticking. Breakdowns are failing. column4: The 2023 investment narrative is already diverging from 2022: Morning Brief
column10: [This article first appeared in the Morning Brief. Get the Morning Brief sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Friday by 6:30 a.m. ET. SubscribeThursday, January 19, 2023Today's newsletter is by Jared Blikre, a reporter focused on the markets on Yahoo Finance. Follow him on Twitter @SPYJared. Read this and more market news on the go with the Yahoo Finance App.Despite Wednesday's losses in the major U.S. indexes, stocks are flying out of the gate in 2023.The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) and S&P 500 (^GSPC) are having their best start to a year since 2019.And in enjoying these gains in the new year, stocks are diverging from the trends that emerged in the second half of 2022. A move that has important implications for investors.Start with the biggest loser of the day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI), which was down 1.81%, or 614 points, on Wednesday, its worst showing in over a month. As of late December, the Dow had outperformed the Nasdaq by 20 percentage points — the most since the dot-com bubble crash two decades prior.Despite this outperformance, however, the Dow ended 2022 down nearly 9%. There were few places for investors to hide in 2022.But Wednesday, the Nasdaq outperformed the Dow by 57 basis points. Particularly notable coming on such a negative day for the market. In the first 11 trading days of the year, the Nasdaq is already up 4.69% compared to the Dow's meager 0.45% gain.If we dive inside the benchmark S&P 500 and look at relative sector performance, 2023's year-to-date sector chart is nearly the inverse of 2022.S&P 500 Sector performance year-to-date through Jan. 18., 2023.(Source: Yahoo Finance)Last year's second-worst-performing sector is this year's best: Consumer Discretionary (XLY).Helping matters are the sector's two largest megacap components — Amazon (AMZN) and Tesla (TSLA) — which are both nicely positive so far in 2023, gaining a little over 4% each.The two other sectors besides consumer discretionary that house some of the market's biggest names — Tech (XLK) and Communication Services (XLC) — are also serving as leaders this year.Story continuesAnd let's not gloss over the strength in Real Estate (XLRE), which is up more than 5% after having just endured one of the most challenging housing markets in a generation last year. Another big narrative shift after 2022.On the flip side, those red sectors in the above heat map — Utilities (XLU), Health Care (XLV), and Consumer Staples (XLP) — were the least-bad sectors after Energy last year. These sectors are also commonly referred to as defensive areas of the market for investors to find shelter in a storm. In the 2023 market, however, it seems safe trades aren't quite safe.The bond market is also confirming moves back into these formerly unloved, growthy areas of the market that took the biggest hits a year ago.On Wednesday, the yield 10-year on U.S. Treasury notes (^TNX) plummeted 16 basis points to 3.375%, a four-month low. All else equal, sinking bond yields favor growth stocks that depend on lower interest rates.And although buying bonds is often seen as investors fleeing to safety, right now the bond bid appears firmly part of a risk on trade.Finally, throw in Wednesday's market reaction to economic news.December retail sales surprised to the downside with a drop of 1.1%, which follows a similar negative print in November. Investors seem to be pricing in this objectively bad news for what it is — bad news — instead of trying to play 4D chess with Jay Powell and the Federal Reserve.Speaking of the Fed, the market's new favorite macro risk assets, bitcoin (BTC-USD) and ethereum (ETH-USD), are each up about 25% this year. Bitcoin and crypto have been particularly volatile around important Fed decisions and inflation data — leading risk markets to the upside at times, and downside at others.Bottom line: Bitcoin is a clear leader this year among the "fringier" parts of the markets, and, currently, the direction is up.Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Returns YTDNow, some of these pockets of the markets have been exhibiting strength since late last year. Under different leadership, this could change.But this is a market starting to show the hands of winners over losers.As Steven Strazza, director of research at All Star Charts tweeted this week: "Breakouts are sticking. column4: President Biden calls for bipartisan unity on protections against growing tech sector
column10: [In his latest op-ed, President Biden has called for political unity from lawmakers to reform Section 230 in order to better regulate ever-expanding tech companies.Video TranscriptDAVE BRIGGS: OK, President Biden calling on Republicans and Democrats in congress to find common ground and unite against big tech. Yahoo Finance Tech Reporter Dan Howley here with more on this. Dan, let me just say, I'm a bit pessimistic that Republicans, less than two years out from presidential election, are going to give the president a win on anything, let alone big tech. But they have begun to turn against big business, so maybe there's an opening.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, there's some common ground here. And I think one of the big things to look at is what Biden really laid out-- he had three different areas. The first has to do with privacy. And, in fact, he writes in this op-ed, we need serious federal protections for Americans' privacy.That means clear limits on how companies can collect, use, and share highly personal data, your internet history, your personal communications, your location, and your health, genetic, and biometric data. He then goes on to say that there needs to be responsibility on the parts of companies for the content that is allowed to be posted by users.That goes into section 230. That's real red meat for Republicans, as well as Democrats. And then there's the idea of getting competition in the tech sector-- so antitrust.These are all things that both sides want to get to work on. They just can't agree on why.SEANA SMITH: Well, yeah, and that's going to be the key issue here going forward. And also, how is big tech looking at this, just in terms of the odds that maybe we will see more regulation-- the fact that GOP and the Democrats, yes, they want change, but they want it in different ways? That seems like a very good sign here, at least for the sector.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, for tech, yes. Obviously, towards the end of the year, they wanted to get some kind of antitrust action moving forward. That just completely fell on its face, right? I don't remember hearing anything happening.Story continuesSo it's not like we're going to get anything coming any time soon. It's probably going to come as individual piecemeal parts of what they originally wanted. So maybe some kind of privacy regulation-- that's been something that both sides have been talking about forever.DAVE BRIGGS: Section 230 has been talked about by both parties.DAN HOWLEY: Right. It depends on what they don't like from each side, right? Republicans say they don't like it because it hinders conservative speech. Democrats say they don't like it because it allows hate speech. So it's these two sides.They both don't like it, but they can't agree on how they want to change it. Now, it's important to point out that Section 230 is the reason why the internet kind of exists as it does right now. So any kind of change at all would dramatically change the internet, at least here in the US, potentially around the world.DAVE BRIGGS: And investors not buying it. If you want to look at stocks, Alphabet up 3%, Amazon up 5%, Meta is basically flat. So they're basically saying, no, we don't think this is likely.SEANA SMITH: Dan, what do you think this means, though, for the M&A landscape for tech in the near-term? Because, certainly, we've heard from a number of analysts, a number of market participants here saying that M&A is really going to be what drives some of this growth here in 2023. If President Biden, taking directly from this op-ed, saying that we need to bring more competition back to the tech sector, you would think we're going to see more of a crackdown, then, on M&A.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, I mean, at least as far as the bigger tech companies go, right? I mean, I don't think Meta is going to be able to go out there and buy anything at all right now. They tried to get that VR company and they were basically just told, no.I don't think we're going to see any kind of stop to the companies-- the Alphabets, the Apples, the Microsofts-- Meta will probably still be able to pick up some companies, but it's not going to be anything that would be in a space where they probably feel like it is under threat from the likes of the FTC. There's also just constant action in that sector-- it's not as though it's just those companies purchasing. Other, smaller companies, though, for those smaller companies, that's really just a big payday for them and that's what they're aiming for.But I don't think that means that we won't see any M&A. It just means that Lina Khan of the FTC, and, obviously, Biden in the White House are going to be keeping an eye on it to see what companies want to do, in particular.DAVE BRIGGS: And the DOJ's antitrust as well-- looks like they're in step there.]

column4: Amazon layoffs: ‘We still like the stock,’ analyst says
column10: [JMP Securities Equity Research Analyst Nick Jones joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the tech sector, Amazon's wave of layoffs, and the performance of Etsy stock.Video Transcript- All right, we want to get you up to speed on another big story of the day, and that's job cuts. Amazon, Vimeo, Stitch Fix, all layoffs today. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy confirming plans to cut 18,000 employees across several teams, including HR and Amazon stores. Vimeo on that list too, announcing another round of layoffs, this time cutting 11% of its workers.Now in an email to the team the CEO noting, quote, "Further deterioration in economic conditions." It has certainly been a tough start to the year, especially in tech, where we already started to see some of those job losses last year. That has carried over to this year. And just in the first couple of days, more than 25,000 jobs have been shed from the tech sector alone.And that's not all, because taking a look at Stitch Fix, which is more so retail consumer facing, they're letting go about 20% of their workforce, Dave. Their CEO Elizabeth Spalding, is also going to be stepping down there. So an executive shakeup, companies really doing all they can in order to cut costs because of this potential recessionary environment that we are in. And people really changing how they're spending and how they're spending their time.- Interesting to see Amazon shares, as you showed, down just-- down at all, because investors cheer these layoffs but down 1 and 1/2%. Usually they cheer layoffs, which tells you they're not nearly enough, and not nearly a big enough picture for the Amazon story, which is largely an AWS story at this point. But I find that Stitch Fix probably the biggest news, because it is non-tech related.We talk a lot about these tech layoffs. That is not going to do the trick. In terms of the Fed, we are not cheering layoffs. But the Fed certainly needs some. And you're talking about 10% of the GDP comes to the tech sector, but only about what 12 million roughly jobs in total in the tech sector. So if all of them were wiped out, it still wouldn't be what the Fed probably needs.Story continuesCompass, the real estate giant, also laid off the third round of layoffs in the last year, just about 450 layoffs. But they continue. They've gone from a $6 billion market cap to a $1 billion company. More bad news for the real estate sector. In the information reporting, Twitter laid off 40 data scientists in terms of advertising.- Yes, certainly a number of layoffs. We want to stick with that story and dive deeper into Amazon's plan to lay off 18,000 workers. For more on that, we want to bring in Nick Jones. He's JMP Securities Equity Research Analyst. Nick, it's great to see you. So let's talk about the impact here on Amazon. Because yes, it's 18,000 jobs. But in the grand scheme of things, when you take into account, Amazon has 1 and 1/2 million employees, it's a very small chunk. But how are you viewing these layoffs and what it could signal ahead?NICK JONES: Yes, I mean, you're right. It's a very small chunk of their employee-- or their workforce. We view it is that they are starting to look at operating income. This is an area that investors are increasingly looking at. They want to see Amazon give better guidance to these numbers as you progress through each quarter.So while we don't think it's really going to move the needle materially, we like that they're focusing on this, and they're making cuts, which should give investors some solace that they are paying attention. But to, as you mentioned earlier in the segment, the stock price isn't reacting. And clearly investors don't see this as meaningful enough today.- Yeah, reacting in fact, the opposite direction as we've become accustomed to, Nick. And it's good to see you. Are there more cuts coming to Amazon in terms of headcount or more cost cutting?NICK JONES: I mean, there could be. Upper funnel trends on retail don't look great. Advertising generally follows retail. So the advertising segment will likely follow. And as enterprises are thinking about making layoffs, and they're also going to think about making cloud investments or maybe just delaying them until they have more macro clarity. So overall there could be more to come.But we like Amazon investing in future technology. We like them investing in growth. So for us, we don't think it has to happen. We still like the stock as it-- from here today. But there could be more to come as upper funnel trends continue to deteriorate.- Nick, what's the level in terms of the scale of the cuts that you would start to get concerned? Because right now you still have an outperform rating on the stock $140 price target. Like what you're saying, you're not too concerned about the news we're getting today. But when does that start potentially affecting your investment thesis?NICK JONES: I think for us it'd be more about their ability to control operating income and kind of say one Q guidance or how they're talking about next year. I don't think they really need to do more cuts. Clearly the trends are indicating that they think they may need to preserve the operating income investors are looking for.If more cuts come, I think that's more likely to be viewed as a positive by investors. That wouldn't concern us more. That probably if anything gets the stock moving higher from here. If operating income really starts to become a problem, the lack of cuts would be more concerning in the coming quarters.- Amazon dropped about half its market cap just last year. What's the catalyst to get things back on track. Because it's still largely an AWS story?NICK JONES: Yes, it is. It's definitely still an AWS story. I mean, we still want to see retail work. I think advertising is underappreciated. But heading into a recession, you know, it's hard to like advertising going into 2023. So really, we need to see AWS start re-accelerating. We need to see retail kind of, estimates need to start increasing on the retail segment.We kind of need to bottom out in terms of estimates and get more visibility on the macro situation. Is the Fed going to continue to increase rates and by how much? I think once we get some visibility into cost of capital, where rates are going, that's when investors can kind of pick their head up and start thinking about what back half of '23 and '24 starts to look like.- And, Nick, I know you cover a number of consumer facing names, eBay, Etsy, Poshmark, all on your list here. What do you think the 2023 has in store here in terms of the significance of the slowdown and what it means for so many consumer facing names?NICK JONES: Yeah, it's going to be a tough set up. Saving rates are declining. They're very low today. So that means discretionary income is going to start decreasing. Within my coverage, we think Etsy has been one of the best performers, with their kind of robust platform, a lot of tech enhancements to keep people coming back and going to different segments.But overall it's really going to be tied to personal consumption expenditure. E-com will continue to gain share, but if discretionary spend starts to decrease, there's going to be overall less spend on retail. That will impact e-com even though they're back to share gains.So it could be a tough first half we think for e-commerce. But we think it's looking better kind of in the back half as we get over easier comps. All that said, we think Etsy is positioned as kind of the best e-commerce marketplace right now.- And to follow back up on Amazon, Andy Jassy could not have been handed this baton at a worse time. They have shed more than a trillion since he took over. Is he, despite all that, making the right moves? Do investors have confidence?NICK JONES: We think so. We think so. I think it's just very much-- the theme I keep hearing talking to investors as you can't fight the Fed. You can't fight macro. I think this is very much a macro Fed driven market. And that's really compressing multiples.We were looking today, most of the multiples of the stocks we cover are well below their five or 10 year average, in many cases below 1 standard deviation below that. Meaning multiples compress materially, close to what recessionary levels look like during the great financial crisis. So I think this is very much a macro dynamic, more so than anything idiosyncratic to what Jassy is doing at the company.- Indeed all right, Nick Jones, JMP Securities, good to see you, man. Thank you.]

column4: The 2023 investment narrative is already diverging from 2022: Morning Brief
column10: [This article first appeared in the Morning Brief. Get the Morning Brief sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Friday by 6:30 a.m. ET. SubscribeThursday, January 19, 2023Today's newsletter is by Jared Blikre, a reporter focused on the markets on Yahoo Finance. Follow him on Twitter @SPYJared. Read this and more market news on the go with the Yahoo Finance App.Despite Wednesday's losses in the major U.S. indexes, stocks are flying out of the gate in 2023.The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) and S&P 500 (^GSPC) are having their best start to a year since 2019.And in enjoying these gains in the new year, stocks are diverging from the trends that emerged in the second half of 2022. A move that has important implications for investors.Start with the biggest loser of the day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI), which was down 1.81%, or 614 points, on Wednesday, its worst showing in over a month. As of late December, the Dow had outperformed the Nasdaq by 20 percentage points — the most since the dot-com bubble crash two decades prior.Despite this outperformance, however, the Dow ended 2022 down nearly 9%. There were few places for investors to hide in 2022.But Wednesday, the Nasdaq outperformed the Dow by 57 basis points. Particularly notable coming on such a negative day for the market. In the first 11 trading days of the year, the Nasdaq is already up 4.69% compared to the Dow's meager 0.45% gain.If we dive inside the benchmark S&P 500 and look at relative sector performance, 2023's year-to-date sector chart is nearly the inverse of 2022.S&P 500 Sector performance year-to-date through Jan. 18., 2023.(Source: Yahoo Finance)Last year's second-worst-performing sector is this year's best: Consumer Discretionary (XLY).Helping matters are the sector's two largest megacap components — Amazon (AMZN) and Tesla (TSLA) — which are both nicely positive so far in 2023, gaining a little over 4% each.The two other sectors besides consumer discretionary that house some of the market's biggest names — Tech (XLK) and Communication Services (XLC) — are also serving as leaders this year.Story continuesAnd let's not gloss over the strength in Real Estate (XLRE), which is up more than 5% after having just endured one of the most challenging housing markets in a generation last year. Another big narrative shift after 2022.On the flip side, those red sectors in the above heat map — Utilities (XLU), Health Care (XLV), and Consumer Staples (XLP) — were the least-bad sectors after Energy last year. These sectors are also commonly referred to as defensive areas of the market for investors to find shelter in a storm. In the 2023 market, however, it seems safe trades aren't quite safe.The bond market is also confirming moves back into these formerly unloved, growthy areas of the market that took the biggest hits a year ago.On Wednesday, the yield 10-year on U.S. Treasury notes (^TNX) plummeted 16 basis points to 3.375%, a four-month low. All else equal, sinking bond yields favor growth stocks that depend on lower interest rates.And although buying bonds is often seen as investors fleeing to safety, right now the bond bid appears firmly part of a risk on trade.Finally, throw in Wednesday's market reaction to economic news.December retail sales surprised to the downside with a drop of 1.1%, which follows a similar negative print in November. Investors seem to be pricing in this objectively bad news for what it is — bad news — instead of trying to play 4D chess with Jay Powell and the Federal Reserve.Speaking of the Fed, the market's new favorite macro risk assets, bitcoin (BTC-USD) and ethereum (ETH-USD), are each up about 25% this year. Bitcoin and crypto have been particularly volatile around important Fed decisions and inflation data — leading risk markets to the upside at times, and downside at others.Bottom line: Bitcoin is a clear leader this year among the "fringier" parts of the markets, and, currently, the direction is up.Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Returns YTDNow, some of these pockets of the markets have been exhibiting strength since late last year. Under different leadership, this could change.But this is a market starting to show the hands of winners over losers.As Steven Strazza, director of research at All Star Charts tweeted this week: "Breakouts are sticking. Breakdowns are failing. It's not bear market behavior."What to Watch TodayEconomy8:30 a.m. ET: Housing Starts, December (1.358 million expected, 1.427 during prior month)8:30 a.m. ET: Building Permits, December (1.365 million expected, 1.342 million during prior month, revised to 1.351 million)8:30 a.m. ET: Housing Starts, month-over-month, December (-4.8% expected, -0.5% during prior month)8:30 a.m. ET: Building Permits, month-over-month, December (1.0% expected, -11.2% during prior month, revised to -10.6%)8:30 a.m. ET: Philadelphia Fed Business Outlook Index, January (-11.0 expected, -13.8 during prior month, revised to -13.7)8:30 a.m. ET: Initial Jobless Claims, week ended Jan. 14 (214,000 expected, 205,000 during prior week)8:30 a.m. ET: Continuing Claims, week ended Jan. 7 (1.655 million expected, 1.634 million during prior week)EarningsNetflix (NFLX), Procter & Gamble (PG), American Airlines (AAL), Comerica Inc. column4: President Biden calls for bipartisan unity on protections against growing tech sector
column10: [In his latest op-ed, President Biden has called for political unity from lawmakers to reform Section 230 in order to better regulate ever-expanding tech companies.Video TranscriptDAVE BRIGGS: OK, President Biden calling on Republicans and Democrats in congress to find common ground and unite against big tech. Yahoo Finance Tech Reporter Dan Howley here with more on this. Dan, let me just say, I'm a bit pessimistic that Republicans, less than two years out from presidential election, are going to give the president a win on anything, let alone big tech. But they have begun to turn against big business, so maybe there's an opening.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, there's some common ground here. And I think one of the big things to look at is what Biden really laid out-- he had three different areas. The first has to do with privacy. And, in fact, he writes in this op-ed, we need serious federal protections for Americans' privacy.That means clear limits on how companies can collect, use, and share highly personal data, your internet history, your personal communications, your location, and your health, genetic, and biometric data. He then goes on to say that there needs to be responsibility on the parts of companies for the content that is allowed to be posted by users.That goes into section 230. That's real red meat for Republicans, as well as Democrats. And then there's the idea of getting competition in the tech sector-- so antitrust.These are all things that both sides want to get to work on. They just can't agree on why.SEANA SMITH: Well, yeah, and that's going to be the key issue here going forward. And also, how is big tech looking at this, just in terms of the odds that maybe we will see more regulation-- the fact that GOP and the Democrats, yes, they want change, but they want it in different ways? That seems like a very good sign here, at least for the sector.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, for tech, yes. Obviously, towards the end of the year, they wanted to get some kind of antitrust action moving forward. That just completely fell on its face, right? I don't remember hearing anything happening.Story continuesSo it's not like we're going to get anything coming any time soon. It's probably going to come as individual piecemeal parts of what they originally wanted. So maybe some kind of privacy regulation-- that's been something that both sides have been talking about forever.DAVE BRIGGS: Section 230 has been talked about by both parties.DAN HOWLEY: Right. It depends on what they don't like from each side, right? Republicans say they don't like it because it hinders conservative speech. Democrats say they don't like it because it allows hate speech. So it's these two sides.They both don't like it, but they can't agree on how they want to change it. Now, it's important to point out that Section 230 is the reason why the internet kind of exists as it does right now. So any kind of change at all would dramatically change the internet, at least here in the US, potentially around the world.DAVE BRIGGS: And investors not buying it. If you want to look at stocks, Alphabet up 3%, Amazon up 5%, Meta is basically flat. So they're basically saying, no, we don't think this is likely.SEANA SMITH: Dan, what do you think this means, though, for the M&A landscape for tech in the near-term? Because, certainly, we've heard from a number of analysts, a number of market participants here saying that M&A is really going to be what drives some of this growth here in 2023. If President Biden, taking directly from this op-ed, saying that we need to bring more competition back to the tech sector, you would think we're going to see more of a crackdown, then, on M&A.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, I mean, at least as far as the bigger tech companies go, right? I mean, I don't think Meta is going to be able to go out there and buy anything at all right now. They tried to get that VR company and they were basically just told, no.I don't think we're going to see any kind of stop to the companies-- the Alphabets, the Apples, the Microsofts-- Meta will probably still be able to pick up some companies, but it's not going to be anything that would be in a space where they probably feel like it is under threat from the likes of the FTC. There's also just constant action in that sector-- it's not as though it's just those companies purchasing. Other, smaller companies, though, for those smaller companies, that's really just a big payday for them and that's what they're aiming for.But I don't think that means that we won't see any M&A. It just means that Lina Khan of the FTC, and, obviously, Biden in the White House are going to be keeping an eye on it to see what companies want to do, in particular.DAVE BRIGGS: And the DOJ's antitrust as well-- looks like they're in step there.]

column4: Amazon layoffs: ‘We still like the stock,’ analyst says
column10: [JMP Securities Equity Research Analyst Nick Jones joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the tech sector, Amazon's wave of layoffs, and the performance of Etsy stock.Video Transcript- All right, we want to get you up to speed on another big story of the day, and that's job cuts. Amazon, Vimeo, Stitch Fix, all layoffs today. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy confirming plans to cut 18,000 employees across several teams, including HR and Amazon stores. Vimeo on that list too, announcing another round of layoffs, this time cutting 11% of its workers.Now in an email to the team the CEO noting, quote, "Further deterioration in economic conditions." It has certainly been a tough start to the year, especially in tech, where we already started to see some of those job losses last year. That has carried over to this year. And just in the first couple of days, more than 25,000 jobs have been shed from the tech sector alone.And that's not all, because taking a look at Stitch Fix, which is more so retail consumer facing, they're letting go about 20% of their workforce, Dave. Their CEO Elizabeth Spalding, is also going to be stepping down there. So an executive shakeup, companies really doing all they can in order to cut costs because of this potential recessionary environment that we are in. And people really changing how they're spending and how they're spending their time.- Interesting to see Amazon shares, as you showed, down just-- down at all, because investors cheer these layoffs but down 1 and 1/2%. Usually they cheer layoffs, which tells you they're not nearly enough, and not nearly a big enough picture for the Amazon story, which is largely an AWS story at this point. But I find that Stitch Fix probably the biggest news, because it is non-tech related.We talk a lot about these tech layoffs. That is not going to do the trick. In terms of the Fed, we are not cheering layoffs. But the Fed certainly needs some. And you're talking about 10% of the GDP comes to the tech sector, but only about what 12 million roughly jobs in total in the tech sector. So if all of them were wiped out, it still wouldn't be what the Fed probably needs.Story continuesCompass, the real estate giant, also laid off the third round of layoffs in the last year, just about 450 layoffs. But they continue. They've gone from a $6 billion market cap to a $1 billion company. More bad news for the real estate sector. In the information reporting, Twitter laid off 40 data scientists in terms of advertising.- Yes, certainly a number of layoffs. We want to stick with that story and dive deeper into Amazon's plan to lay off 18,000 workers. For more on that, we want to bring in Nick Jones. He's JMP Securities Equity Research Analyst. Nick, it's great to see you. So let's talk about the impact here on Amazon. Because yes, it's 18,000 jobs. But in the grand scheme of things, when you take into account, Amazon has 1 and 1/2 million employees, it's a very small chunk. But how are you viewing these layoffs and what it could signal ahead?NICK JONES: Yes, I mean, you're right. It's a very small chunk of their employee-- or their workforce. We view it is that they are starting to look at operating income. This is an area that investors are increasingly looking at. They want to see Amazon give better guidance to these numbers as you progress through each quarter.So while we don't think it's really going to move the needle materially, we like that they're focusing on this, and they're making cuts, which should give investors some solace that they are paying attention. But to, as you mentioned earlier in the segment, the stock price isn't reacting. And clearly investors don't see this as meaningful enough today.- Yeah, reacting in fact, the opposite direction as we've become accustomed to, Nick. And it's good to see you. Are there more cuts coming to Amazon in terms of headcount or more cost cutting?NICK JONES: I mean, there could be. Upper funnel trends on retail don't look great. Advertising generally follows retail. So the advertising segment will likely follow. And as enterprises are thinking about making layoffs, and they're also going to think about making cloud investments or maybe just delaying them until they have more macro clarity. So overall there could be more to come.But we like Amazon investing in future technology. We like them investing in growth. So for us, we don't think it has to happen. We still like the stock as it-- from here today. But there could be more to come as upper funnel trends continue to deteriorate.- Nick, what's the level in terms of the scale of the cuts that you would start to get concerned? Because right now you still have an outperform rating on the stock $140 price target. Like what you're saying, you're not too concerned about the news we're getting today. But when does that start potentially affecting your investment thesis?NICK JONES: I think for us it'd be more about their ability to control operating income and kind of say one Q guidance or how they're talking about next year. I don't think they really need to do more cuts. Clearly the trends are indicating that they think they may need to preserve the operating income investors are looking for.If more cuts come, I think that's more likely to be viewed as a positive by investors. That wouldn't concern us more. That probably if anything gets the stock moving higher from here. If operating income really starts to become a problem, the lack of cuts would be more concerning in the coming quarters.- Amazon dropped about half its market cap just last year. What's the catalyst to get things back on track. Because it's still largely an AWS story?NICK JONES: Yes, it is. It's definitely still an AWS story. I mean, we still want to see retail work. I think advertising is underappreciated. But heading into a recession, you know, it's hard to like advertising going into 2023. So really, we need to see AWS start re-accelerating. We need to see retail kind of, estimates need to start increasing on the retail segment.We kind of need to bottom out in terms of estimates and get more visibility on the macro situation. Is the Fed going to continue to increase rates and by how much? I think once we get some visibility into cost of capital, where rates are going, that's when investors can kind of pick their head up and start thinking about what back half of '23 and '24 starts to look like.- And, Nick, I know you cover a number of consumer facing names, eBay, Etsy, Poshmark, all on your list here. What do you think the 2023 has in store here in terms of the significance of the slowdown and what it means for so many consumer facing names?NICK JONES: Yeah, it's going to be a tough set up. Saving rates are declining. They're very low today. So that means discretionary income is going to start decreasing. Within my coverage, we think Etsy has been one of the best performers, with their kind of robust platform, a lot of tech enhancements to keep people coming back and going to different segments.But overall it's really going to be tied to personal consumption expenditure. E-com will continue to gain share, but if discretionary spend starts to decrease, there's going to be overall less spend on retail. That will impact e-com even though they're back to share gains.So it could be a tough first half we think for e-commerce. But we think it's looking better kind of in the back half as we get over easier comps. All that said, we think Etsy is positioned as kind of the best e-commerce marketplace right now.- And to follow back up on Amazon, Andy Jassy could not have been handed this baton at a worse time. They have shed more than a trillion since he took over. Is he, despite all that, making the right moves? Do investors have confidence?NICK JONES: We think so. We think so. I think it's just very much-- the theme I keep hearing talking to investors as you can't fight the Fed. You can't fight macro. I think this is very much a macro Fed driven market. And that's really compressing multiples.We were looking today, most of the multiples of the stocks we cover are well below their five or 10 year average, in many cases below 1 standard deviation below that. Meaning multiples compress materially, close to what recessionary levels look like during the great financial crisis. So I think this is very much a macro dynamic, more so than anything idiosyncratic to what Jassy is doing at the company.- Indeed all right, Nick Jones, JMP Securities, good to see you, man. Thank you.]

column4: Financial Industry ETFs Slump as Banks Report Mixed 4Q Earnings
column10: [Exchange-traded funds that focus on banks and asset managers are tumbling after a week of weak earnings and warnings of impending economic headwinds. Shares of three of the largest ETFs tracking the financial sector—the Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF), the Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH) and the Fidelity MSCI Financials Index ETF (FNCL)—all dipped 1.2% on Thursday after posting consecutive losses during the week.  Rough Ride for XLF, VFH, FNCLSource: Bloomberg Large asset managers reported a mix of fourth-quarter earnings results. JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America Corp. and Charles Schwab Corp. boasted year-over-year revenue increases as balance sheets were buoyed by net interest income. Other firms fared less well: Revenue at BlackRock Inc., the world’s biggest ETF issuer, plummeted 18% year over year, and Goldman Sachs Inc. posted its largest earnings miss in a decade. All five companies are within the top 10 holdings in XLF, VFH and FNCL. Still, executives are cautioning of a coming economic downturn, despite stocks bouncing back after 2022’s double-digit declines. “We still do not know the ultimate effect of the headwinds coming from geopolitical tensions,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said during the bank’s fourth-quarter earnings call last week. He listed impediments to growth such as “war in Ukraine, the vulnerable state of energy and food supplies, persistent inflation that is eroding purchasing power and has pushed interest rates higher, and the unprecedented quantitative tightening.” In preparation, banks are bolstering loan loss provisions, cash reserves that banks set aside to cover problem loans that are unlikely to see repayment. Bank of America, the second largest bank in the U.S., has set aside $403 million to cover possible bad loans, with CEO Brian Moynihan alluding to an "increasingly slowing economic environment” during the firm’s quarterly earnings call with analysts and investors. column4: The 2023 investment narrative is already diverging from 2022: Morning Brief
column10: [This article first appeared in the Morning Brief. Get the Morning Brief sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Friday by 6:30 a.m. ET. SubscribeThursday, January 19, 2023Today's newsletter is by Jared Blikre, a reporter focused on the markets on Yahoo Finance. Follow him on Twitter @SPYJared. Read this and more market news on the go with the Yahoo Finance App.Despite Wednesday's losses in the major U.S. indexes, stocks are flying out of the gate in 2023.The Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) and S&P 500 (^GSPC) are having their best start to a year since 2019.And in enjoying these gains in the new year, stocks are diverging from the trends that emerged in the second half of 2022. A move that has important implications for investors.Start with the biggest loser of the day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI), which was down 1.81%, or 614 points, on Wednesday, its worst showing in over a month. As of late December, the Dow had outperformed the Nasdaq by 20 percentage points — the most since the dot-com bubble crash two decades prior.Despite this outperformance, however, the Dow ended 2022 down nearly 9%. There were few places for investors to hide in 2022.But Wednesday, the Nasdaq outperformed the Dow by 57 basis points. Particularly notable coming on such a negative day for the market. In the first 11 trading days of the year, the Nasdaq is already up 4.69% compared to the Dow's meager 0.45% gain.If we dive inside the benchmark S&P 500 and look at relative sector performance, 2023's year-to-date sector chart is nearly the inverse of 2022.S&P 500 Sector performance year-to-date through Jan. 18., 2023.(Source: Yahoo Finance)Last year's second-worst-performing sector is this year's best: Consumer Discretionary (XLY).Helping matters are the sector's two largest megacap components — Amazon (AMZN) and Tesla (TSLA) — which are both nicely positive so far in 2023, gaining a little over 4% each.The two other sectors besides consumer discretionary that house some of the market's biggest names — Tech (XLK) and Communication Services (XLC) — are also serving as leaders this year.Story continuesAnd let's not gloss over the strength in Real Estate (XLRE), which is up more than 5% after having just endured one of the most challenging housing markets in a generation last year. Another big narrative shift after 2022.On the flip side, those red sectors in the above heat map — Utilities (XLU), Health Care (XLV), and Consumer Staples (XLP) — were the least-bad sectors after Energy last year. These sectors are also commonly referred to as defensive areas of the market for investors to find shelter in a storm. In the 2023 market, however, it seems safe trades aren't quite safe.The bond market is also confirming moves back into these formerly unloved, growthy areas of the market that took the biggest hits a year ago.On Wednesday, the yield 10-year on U.S. Treasury notes (^TNX) plummeted 16 basis points to 3.375%, a four-month low. All else equal, sinking bond yields favor growth stocks that depend on lower interest rates.And although buying bonds is often seen as investors fleeing to safety, right now the bond bid appears firmly part of a risk on trade.Finally, throw in Wednesday's market reaction to economic news.December retail sales surprised to the downside with a drop of 1.1%, which follows a similar negative print in November. Investors seem to be pricing in this objectively bad news for what it is — bad news — instead of trying to play 4D chess with Jay Powell and the Federal Reserve.Speaking of the Fed, the market's new favorite macro risk assets, bitcoin (BTC-USD) and ethereum (ETH-USD), are each up about 25% this year. Bitcoin and crypto have been particularly volatile around important Fed decisions and inflation data — leading risk markets to the upside at times, and downside at others.Bottom line: Bitcoin is a clear leader this year among the "fringier" parts of the markets, and, currently, the direction is up.Bitcoin and Cryptocurrency Returns YTDNow, some of these pockets of the markets have been exhibiting strength since late last year. Under different leadership, this could change.But this is a market starting to show the hands of winners over losers.As Steven Strazza, director of research at All Star Charts tweeted this week: "Breakouts are sticking. Breakdowns are failing. It's not bear market behavior."What to Watch TodayEconomy8:30 a.m. ET: Housing Starts, December (1.358 million expected, 1.427 during prior month)8:30 a.m. ET: Building Permits, December (1.365 million expected, 1.342 million during prior month, revised to 1.351 million)8:30 a.m. ET: Housing Starts, month-over-month, December (-4.8% expected, -0.5% during prior month)8:30 a.m. ET: Building Permits, month-over-month, December (1.0% expected, -11.2% during prior month, revised to -10.6%)8:30 a.m. ET: Philadelphia Fed Business Outlook Index, January (-11.0 expected, -13.8 during prior month, revised to -13.7)8:30 a.m. ET: Initial Jobless Claims, week ended Jan. 14 (214,000 expected, 205,000 during prior week)8:30 a.m. ET: Continuing Claims, week ended Jan. 7 (1.655 million expected, 1.634 million during prior week)EarningsNetflix (NFLX), Procter & Gamble (PG), American Airlines (AAL), Comerica Inc. column4: President Biden calls for bipartisan unity on protections against growing tech sector
column10: [In his latest op-ed, President Biden has called for political unity from lawmakers to reform Section 230 in order to better regulate ever-expanding tech companies.Video TranscriptDAVE BRIGGS: OK, President Biden calling on Republicans and Democrats in congress to find common ground and unite against big tech. Yahoo Finance Tech Reporter Dan Howley here with more on this. Dan, let me just say, I'm a bit pessimistic that Republicans, less than two years out from presidential election, are going to give the president a win on anything, let alone big tech. But they have begun to turn against big business, so maybe there's an opening.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, there's some common ground here. And I think one of the big things to look at is what Biden really laid out-- he had three different areas. The first has to do with privacy. And, in fact, he writes in this op-ed, we need serious federal protections for Americans' privacy.That means clear limits on how companies can collect, use, and share highly personal data, your internet history, your personal communications, your location, and your health, genetic, and biometric data. He then goes on to say that there needs to be responsibility on the parts of companies for the content that is allowed to be posted by users.That goes into section 230. That's real red meat for Republicans, as well as Democrats. And then there's the idea of getting competition in the tech sector-- so antitrust.These are all things that both sides want to get to work on. They just can't agree on why.SEANA SMITH: Well, yeah, and that's going to be the key issue here going forward. And also, how is big tech looking at this, just in terms of the odds that maybe we will see more regulation-- the fact that GOP and the Democrats, yes, they want change, but they want it in different ways? That seems like a very good sign here, at least for the sector.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, for tech, yes. Obviously, towards the end of the year, they wanted to get some kind of antitrust action moving forward. That just completely fell on its face, right? I don't remember hearing anything happening.Story continuesSo it's not like we're going to get anything coming any time soon. It's probably going to come as individual piecemeal parts of what they originally wanted. So maybe some kind of privacy regulation-- that's been something that both sides have been talking about forever.DAVE BRIGGS: Section 230 has been talked about by both parties.DAN HOWLEY: Right. It depends on what they don't like from each side, right? Republicans say they don't like it because it hinders conservative speech. Democrats say they don't like it because it allows hate speech. So it's these two sides.They both don't like it, but they can't agree on how they want to change it. Now, it's important to point out that Section 230 is the reason why the internet kind of exists as it does right now. So any kind of change at all would dramatically change the internet, at least here in the US, potentially around the world.DAVE BRIGGS: And investors not buying it. If you want to look at stocks, Alphabet up 3%, Amazon up 5%, Meta is basically flat. So they're basically saying, no, we don't think this is likely.SEANA SMITH: Dan, what do you think this means, though, for the M&A landscape for tech in the near-term? Because, certainly, we've heard from a number of analysts, a number of market participants here saying that M&A is really going to be what drives some of this growth here in 2023. If President Biden, taking directly from this op-ed, saying that we need to bring more competition back to the tech sector, you would think we're going to see more of a crackdown, then, on M&A.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, I mean, at least as far as the bigger tech companies go, right? I mean, I don't think Meta is going to be able to go out there and buy anything at all right now. They tried to get that VR company and they were basically just told, no.I don't think we're going to see any kind of stop to the companies-- the Alphabets, the Apples, the Microsofts-- Meta will probably still be able to pick up some companies, but it's not going to be anything that would be in a space where they probably feel like it is under threat from the likes of the FTC. There's also just constant action in that sector-- it's not as though it's just those companies purchasing. Other, smaller companies, though, for those smaller companies, that's really just a big payday for them and that's what they're aiming for.But I don't think that means that we won't see any M&A. It just means that Lina Khan of the FTC, and, obviously, Biden in the White House are going to be keeping an eye on it to see what companies want to do, in particular.DAVE BRIGGS: And the DOJ's antitrust as well-- looks like they're in step there.]

column4: Earnings: What to expect from big banks this week
column10: [Yahoo Finance Live anchors discuss the expectations for big bank earnings this week, as well as news that Goldman Sachs plans to cut 3,200 jobs.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: JPMorgan, Citigroup, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo are among the names that will be reporting their fourth-quarter earnings this Friday. Investors will be keeping an eye on how their mortgage businesses are holding up and listening for signs of optimism on the broader economy. Lots to unpack here with these bank earnings.Guys, is this the quarter where JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon again brings out the warning on the state of the economy? He certainly could. He's been, I think, very out in front warning about where this economy might go in 2023. Is it also the quarter where JPMorgan starts to pull back on some of its tech investments, given the slowing economy? So those are a couple of things I'm watching as pertains to JPM.And then, of course, on news today of Goldman cutting 3,200 jobs. We knew it was coming, but still to see it is, I would say, concerning, and how does how does that CEO, David Solomon, get on that earnings call and project his business looking forward?BRAD SMITH: Yeah, those job cuts coming after we had already seen from JP Morgan and some of the other banks as well, even prior to or during the holiday season, saying that, hey, we're going to need to roll back on some of the bonuses, and that really kind of brings into question what the total compensation package for the existing and the retained base of employees would look like going forward as the banks are really waiting for deal making to come back in full force, waiting to see where investment banking really kind of regains some type of strength given some of the equity-market declines that we had seen in last year.And so with all of that in mind, this earnings period and what they forecast, perhaps, is going to be the biggest kind of takeaway item and what they're seeing in terms of deal making and where they're going to be able to drum up some type of demand for their investment-banking products as well.Story continuesJULIE HYMAN: Yeah, when we look at the Goldman news this morning, it reminds me a little bit of what we've seen from technology because part of it is sort of a pandemic payback, if you will. That is Goldman Sachs usually does an annual culling of its underperformers. It cuts them. Didn't really do that during the pandemic. So part of this is sort of now a delayed reaction, a delayed cutting of some of those folks. That's at least some of what is going on there. But we are perhaps going to hear more about cutting from these companies, especially given that maybe they're not totally prepared for what may be coming at this point.For example, Deutsche Bank last week downgrading Bank of America, JP Morgan, and Truist saying that bank stocks have yet to fully price in a US recession. So are investors fully accounting for the effect this could have on the banks? Are the banks themselves fully accounting for the effect? I think we're going to get lots of discussion around those issues.BRIAN SOZZI: Right. It seems like there's a disconnect, Julie, because I'm looking at some Morgan Stanley price-target changes ahead of earnings. They are cutting estimates on Citigroup and Goldman Sachs pretty significantly.But if you go pull up the KBW Bank Index, as we're showing here, I mean, these stocks have gone nowhere-- really nowhere over the past year despite rising yields, and theoretically that should be good for profit margins. I would argue that chart is suggesting, you know, we're in a recession at some point this year, and that impacts a lot of the businesses beyond deal making for the banks.BRAD SMITH: It runs a little bit counter to what we typically see from some bank activity, at least, during a rising interest-rate environment. They typically would be more beneficiary where they can get more money or earn more from the difference between some of the spreads in their loans.And I think for right now, they're still trying to manage what many other businesses are in trying to understand exactly what their cost structures look like. The cut that we're seeing at Goldman is roughly double what we had seen at Morgan Stanley. That was about 1,600 employees there. And so exactly the number of people that they need in order to continue the operations or the business as usual when business right now isn't kind of that usual operating procedure, if you will, too.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah,. Just to take a step back, if you look at the big businesses of the banks, right-- net interest margin, the difference between what they put out and what they take in, basically, and what they lend, that's going to obviously be a big focus this year. Fee income related to everything from mortgage servicing to the deal making that we were talking about, all of these things are going to be in flux this year and are difficult to predict, I think.]

column4: Amazon layoffs: ‘We still like the stock,’ analyst says
column10: [JMP Securities Equity Research Analyst Nick Jones joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the tech sector, Amazon's wave of layoffs, and the performance of Etsy stock.Video Transcript- All right, we want to get you up to speed on another big story of the day, and that's job cuts. Amazon, Vimeo, Stitch Fix, all layoffs today. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy confirming plans to cut 18,000 employees across several teams, including HR and Amazon stores. Vimeo on that list too, announcing another round of layoffs, this time cutting 11% of its workers.Now in an email to the team the CEO noting, quote, "Further deterioration in economic conditions." It has certainly been a tough start to the year, especially in tech, where we already started to see some of those job losses last year. That has carried over to this year. And just in the first couple of days, more than 25,000 jobs have been shed from the tech sector alone.And that's not all, because taking a look at Stitch Fix, which is more so retail consumer facing, they're letting go about 20% of their workforce, Dave. Their CEO Elizabeth Spalding, is also going to be stepping down there. So an executive shakeup, companies really doing all they can in order to cut costs because of this potential recessionary environment that we are in. And people really changing how they're spending and how they're spending their time.- Interesting to see Amazon shares, as you showed, down just-- down at all, because investors cheer these layoffs but down 1 and 1/2%. Usually they cheer layoffs, which tells you they're not nearly enough, and not nearly a big enough picture for the Amazon story, which is largely an AWS story at this point. But I find that Stitch Fix probably the biggest news, because it is non-tech related.We talk a lot about these tech layoffs. That is not going to do the trick. In terms of the Fed, we are not cheering layoffs. But the Fed certainly needs some. And you're talking about 10% of the GDP comes to the tech sector, but only about what 12 million roughly jobs in total in the tech sector. So if all of them were wiped out, it still wouldn't be what the Fed probably needs.Story continuesCompass, the real estate giant, also laid off the third round of layoffs in the last year, just about 450 layoffs. But they continue. They've gone from a $6 billion market cap to a $1 billion company. More bad news for the real estate sector. In the information reporting, Twitter laid off 40 data scientists in terms of advertising.- Yes, certainly a number of layoffs. We want to stick with that story and dive deeper into Amazon's plan to lay off 18,000 workers. For more on that, we want to bring in Nick Jones. He's JMP Securities Equity Research Analyst. Nick, it's great to see you. So let's talk about the impact here on Amazon. Because yes, it's 18,000 jobs. But in the grand scheme of things, when you take into account, Amazon has 1 and 1/2 million employees, it's a very small chunk. But how are you viewing these layoffs and what it could signal ahead?NICK JONES: Yes, I mean, you're right. It's a very small chunk of their employee-- or their workforce. We view it is that they are starting to look at operating income. This is an area that investors are increasingly looking at. They want to see Amazon give better guidance to these numbers as you progress through each quarter.So while we don't think it's really going to move the needle materially, we like that they're focusing on this, and they're making cuts, which should give investors some solace that they are paying attention. But to, as you mentioned earlier in the segment, the stock price isn't reacting. And clearly investors don't see this as meaningful enough today.- Yeah, reacting in fact, the opposite direction as we've become accustomed to, Nick. And it's good to see you. Are there more cuts coming to Amazon in terms of headcount or more cost cutting?NICK JONES: I mean, there could be. Upper funnel trends on retail don't look great. Advertising generally follows retail. So the advertising segment will likely follow. And as enterprises are thinking about making layoffs, and they're also going to think about making cloud investments or maybe just delaying them until they have more macro clarity. So overall there could be more to come.But we like Amazon investing in future technology. We like them investing in growth. So for us, we don't think it has to happen. We still like the stock as it-- from here today. But there could be more to come as upper funnel trends continue to deteriorate.- Nick, what's the level in terms of the scale of the cuts that you would start to get concerned? Because right now you still have an outperform rating on the stock $140 price target. Like what you're saying, you're not too concerned about the news we're getting today. But when does that start potentially affecting your investment thesis?NICK JONES: I think for us it'd be more about their ability to control operating income and kind of say one Q guidance or how they're talking about next year. I don't think they really need to do more cuts. Clearly the trends are indicating that they think they may need to preserve the operating income investors are looking for.If more cuts come, I think that's more likely to be viewed as a positive by investors. That wouldn't concern us more. That probably if anything gets the stock moving higher from here. If operating income really starts to become a problem, the lack of cuts would be more concerning in the coming quarters.- Amazon dropped about half its market cap just last year. What's the catalyst to get things back on track. Because it's still largely an AWS story?NICK JONES: Yes, it is. It's definitely still an AWS story. I mean, we still want to see retail work. I think advertising is underappreciated. But heading into a recession, you know, it's hard to like advertising going into 2023. So really, we need to see AWS start re-accelerating. We need to see retail kind of, estimates need to start increasing on the retail segment.We kind of need to bottom out in terms of estimates and get more visibility on the macro situation. Is the Fed going to continue to increase rates and by how much? I think once we get some visibility into cost of capital, where rates are going, that's when investors can kind of pick their head up and start thinking about what back half of '23 and '24 starts to look like.- And, Nick, I know you cover a number of consumer facing names, eBay, Etsy, Poshmark, all on your list here. What do you think the 2023 has in store here in terms of the significance of the slowdown and what it means for so many consumer facing names?NICK JONES: Yeah, it's going to be a tough set up. Saving rates are declining. They're very low today. So that means discretionary income is going to start decreasing. Within my coverage, we think Etsy has been one of the best performers, with their kind of robust platform, a lot of tech enhancements to keep people coming back and going to different segments.But overall it's really going to be tied to personal consumption expenditure. E-com will continue to gain share, but if discretionary spend starts to decrease, there's going to be overall less spend on retail. That will impact e-com even though they're back to share gains.So it could be a tough first half we think for e-commerce. But we think it's looking better kind of in the back half as we get over easier comps. All that said, we think Etsy is positioned as kind of the best e-commerce marketplace right now.- And to follow back up on Amazon, Andy Jassy could not have been handed this baton at a worse time. They have shed more than a trillion since he took over. Is he, despite all that, making the right moves? Do investors have confidence?NICK JONES: We think so. We think so. I think it's just very much-- the theme I keep hearing talking to investors as you can't fight the Fed. You can't fight macro. I think this is very much a macro Fed driven market. And that's really compressing multiples.We were looking today, most of the multiples of the stocks we cover are well below their five or 10 year average, in many cases below 1 standard deviation below that. Meaning multiples compress materially, close to what recessionary levels look like during the great financial crisis. So I think this is very much a macro dynamic, more so than anything idiosyncratic to what Jassy is doing at the company.- Indeed all right, Nick Jones, JMP Securities, good to see you, man. Thank you.]

column4: Financial Industry ETFs Slump as Banks Report Mixed 4Q Earnings
column10: [Exchange-traded funds that focus on banks and asset managers are tumbling after a week of weak earnings and warnings of impending economic headwinds. Shares of three of the largest ETFs tracking the financial sector—the Financial Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLF), the Vanguard Financials ETF (VFH) and the Fidelity MSCI Financials Index ETF (FNCL)—all dipped 1.2% on Thursday after posting consecutive losses during the week.  Rough Ride for XLF, VFH, FNCLSource: Bloomberg Large asset managers reported a mix of fourth-quarter earnings results. JPMorgan Chase & Co., Bank of America Corp. and Charles Schwab Corp. boasted year-over-year revenue increases as balance sheets were buoyed by net interest income. Other firms fared less well: Revenue at BlackRock Inc., the world’s biggest ETF issuer, plummeted 18% year over year, and Goldman Sachs Inc. posted its largest earnings miss in a decade. All five companies are within the top 10 holdings in XLF, VFH and FNCL. Still, executives are cautioning of a coming economic downturn, despite stocks bouncing back after 2022’s double-digit declines. “We still do not know the ultimate effect of the headwinds coming from geopolitical tensions,” JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said during the bank’s fourth-quarter earnings call last week. column4: President Biden calls for bipartisan unity on protections against growing tech sector
column10: [In his latest op-ed, President Biden has called for political unity from lawmakers to reform Section 230 in order to better regulate ever-expanding tech companies.Video TranscriptDAVE BRIGGS: OK, President Biden calling on Republicans and Democrats in congress to find common ground and unite against big tech. Yahoo Finance Tech Reporter Dan Howley here with more on this. Dan, let me just say, I'm a bit pessimistic that Republicans, less than two years out from presidential election, are going to give the president a win on anything, let alone big tech. But they have begun to turn against big business, so maybe there's an opening.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, there's some common ground here. And I think one of the big things to look at is what Biden really laid out-- he had three different areas. The first has to do with privacy. And, in fact, he writes in this op-ed, we need serious federal protections for Americans' privacy.That means clear limits on how companies can collect, use, and share highly personal data, your internet history, your personal communications, your location, and your health, genetic, and biometric data. He then goes on to say that there needs to be responsibility on the parts of companies for the content that is allowed to be posted by users.That goes into section 230. That's real red meat for Republicans, as well as Democrats. And then there's the idea of getting competition in the tech sector-- so antitrust.These are all things that both sides want to get to work on. They just can't agree on why.SEANA SMITH: Well, yeah, and that's going to be the key issue here going forward. And also, how is big tech looking at this, just in terms of the odds that maybe we will see more regulation-- the fact that GOP and the Democrats, yes, they want change, but they want it in different ways? That seems like a very good sign here, at least for the sector.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, for tech, yes. Obviously, towards the end of the year, they wanted to get some kind of antitrust action moving forward. That just completely fell on its face, right? I don't remember hearing anything happening.Story continuesSo it's not like we're going to get anything coming any time soon. It's probably going to come as individual piecemeal parts of what they originally wanted. So maybe some kind of privacy regulation-- that's been something that both sides have been talking about forever.DAVE BRIGGS: Section 230 has been talked about by both parties.DAN HOWLEY: Right. It depends on what they don't like from each side, right? Republicans say they don't like it because it hinders conservative speech. Democrats say they don't like it because it allows hate speech. So it's these two sides.They both don't like it, but they can't agree on how they want to change it. Now, it's important to point out that Section 230 is the reason why the internet kind of exists as it does right now. So any kind of change at all would dramatically change the internet, at least here in the US, potentially around the world.DAVE BRIGGS: And investors not buying it. If you want to look at stocks, Alphabet up 3%, Amazon up 5%, Meta is basically flat. So they're basically saying, no, we don't think this is likely.SEANA SMITH: Dan, what do you think this means, though, for the M&A landscape for tech in the near-term? Because, certainly, we've heard from a number of analysts, a number of market participants here saying that M&A is really going to be what drives some of this growth here in 2023. If President Biden, taking directly from this op-ed, saying that we need to bring more competition back to the tech sector, you would think we're going to see more of a crackdown, then, on M&A.DAN HOWLEY: Yeah, I mean, at least as far as the bigger tech companies go, right? I mean, I don't think Meta is going to be able to go out there and buy anything at all right now. They tried to get that VR company and they were basically just told, no.I don't think we're going to see any kind of stop to the companies-- the Alphabets, the Apples, the Microsofts-- Meta will probably still be able to pick up some companies, but it's not going to be anything that would be in a space where they probably feel like it is under threat from the likes of the FTC. There's also just constant action in that sector-- it's not as though it's just those companies purchasing. Other, smaller companies, though, for those smaller companies, that's really just a big payday for them and that's what they're aiming for.But I don't think that means that we won't see any M&A. It just means that Lina Khan of the FTC, and, obviously, Biden in the White House are going to be keeping an eye on it to see what companies want to do, in particular.DAVE BRIGGS: And the DOJ's antitrust as well-- looks like they're in step there.]

column4: Earnings: What to expect from big banks this week
column10: [Yahoo Finance Live anchors discuss the expectations for big bank earnings this week, as well as news that Goldman Sachs plans to cut 3,200 jobs.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: JPMorgan, Citigroup, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo are among the names that will be reporting their fourth-quarter earnings this Friday. So part of this is sort of now a delayed reaction, a delayed cutting of some of those folks. That's at least some of what is going on there. But we are perhaps going to hear more about cutting from these companies, especially given that maybe they're not totally prepared for what may be coming at this point.For example, Deutsche Bank last week downgrading Bank of America, JP Morgan, and Truist saying that bank stocks have yet to fully price in a US recession. It seems like there's a disconnect, Julie, because I'm looking at some Morgan Stanley price-target changes ahead of earnings. Fee income related to everything from mortgage servicing to the deal making that we were talking about, all of these things are going to be in flux this year and are difficult to predict, I think.]
